e-4422.knowledge_point: Calculating a Determinant After Switching Two Rows
e-4422.problem: Suppose $A$ is a $3 \times 3$ matrix and $\det (A) = -16.$ The matrix $B$ is obtained from $A$ by applying the elementary row operation $R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2$ (switching the first and the second rows). What is the value of $\det(B)?$
e-4422.worked_solution:
Since swapping any two rows changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite sign, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B) & =-det(A) \\  & =-(-16) \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

e-4423.knowledge_point: Calculating a Determinant After Multiplying a Row by a Number
e-4423.problem: Suppose $A$ is a $6 \times 6$ matrix and $\det(A) = 32.$ The matrix $B$ is obtained from $A$ by applying the elementary row operation $R_3:= \dfrac{1}{8} R_3$. What is the value of $\det(B)?$
e-4423.worked_solution:
The row operation applied to $A$ consists of multiplying a row by the number $\dfrac{1}{8}.$

When we do this, the determinant is multiplied by the same number. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B) & =\frac{1}{8}det(A) \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot 32 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

e-6148.knowledge_point: Calculating a Determinant After Multiplying a Matrix by a Scalar
e-6148.problem: Suppose $A$ is a $4\times4$ matrix and $\det(A)=5.$ What is the value of $\det(2A)?$
e-6148.worked_solution:
Multiplying a $n\times n$ matrix by a scalar $k$ is equivalent to multiplying each row by $k,$ and this occurs $n$ times. This leads to the result

$$
\begin{aligned}det(k\cdot A)={k}^{n}\cdot det(A).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have $k=2$ and $n=4.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}det(2A) & ={2}^{4}\cdot det(A) \\  & =16\cdot 5 \\  & =80.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 12
after.problem: Suppose $B$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $det(B)=-4.$ What is the value of $det(5B)?$
after.worked_solution:
Multiplying a $n\times n$ matrix by a scalar $k$ is equivalent to multiplying each row by $k,$ and this occurs $n$ times. This leads to the result

$$
\begin{aligned}det(k\cdot B)={k}^{n}\cdot det(B).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have $k=5$ and $n=2.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}det(5B) & ={5}^{2}\cdot det(B) \\  & =25\cdot (-4) \\  & =-100.\end{aligned}
$$
